name: Kemalism
info: Kemalism is the nationalist and secular ideology of Mustafa Kemal Atatürk, founder of the Republic of Turkey in 1923, whose six principles drove sweeping reforms that separated the new state from its Ottoman past and remain its founding creed.

facts.thinkers: Mustafa Kemal Atatürk, founder and first president of the Republic of Turkey; Yakup Kadri Karaosmanoğlu, Bozkurt and Ahmet Cevat Emre, to whom the term is attributed; forerunners in the Young Ottomans and the Committee of Union and Progress
facts.texts: Atatürk’s speech Nutuk; the 1924 Constitution (“republican, nationalist, attached to the people, interventionist, secular, and revolutionary”); the amendment of 5 February 1937 that made the six principles state ideology; the constitutions of 1961 and 1982
facts.ideas: republicanism and popular sovereignty; populism, with national unity above class; nationalism, a nation state of citizens in place of the Ottoman millets; laicism, after French laïcité, with state control of religion; statism, the state directing the economy; reformism, the reforms held irreversible
facts.today: the founding ideology of the Republic of Turkey, whose 1982 constitution declares it “loyal to the nationalism of Atatürk”; the Republican People’s Party (CHP), founded by Atatürk and centre-left since the 1960s; by the early 21st century most Kemalists still held to the six principles, while others sought to reduce its statism

t: Kemalism is the ideology of Mustafa Kemal Atatürk, founder of the Republic of Turkey in 1923, summed up in the six principles of the Six Arrows: republicanism, populism, nationalism, laicism, statism and reformism.

Its reforms abolished the caliphate in 1924, replaced sharia with an adapted Swiss Civil Code in 1926 and struck Islam from the constitution as the state religion in 1928, and in 1937 the six principles became state ideology.
It became a model for modernizers from Afghanistan and Iran to Tunisia, while its nationalism denied the identity of the Kurds for decades and treated non-Muslims as second-class citizens.
dyk: Under the Kemalist reforms Turks had to adopt surnames, the weekly day of rest moved from Friday to Sunday, and wearing the fez, which Atatürk saw as a tie to the Ottoman past, was penalized.
ev: The Young Turk Revolution reinstates the Ottoman constitution; Atatürk is a member of the Committee of Union and Progress
Atatürk founds the Republican People’s Party, and the Republic of Turkey is declared
The Ottoman caliphate is abolished, and the office of Shaykh al-Islām is replaced by the Presidency of Religious Affairs
The mejelle and sharia codes give way to an adapted Swiss Civil Code and a penal code on German and Italian models
The article naming Islam as the established religion of Turkey is removed from the constitution
Yakup Kadri Karaosmanoğlu uses the word Kemalism for the principles of the Turkish path to modernity
The six principles are written into the constitution as state ideology
A new constitution after the military coup of 1980 declares the Republic loyal to the nationalism of Atatürk

sections.origins:
Kemalism grew out of a century of Ottoman reform. Attempts to stave off the empire’s collapse began chiefly with the 19th-century Tanzimat reforms; the Young Ottomans of the mid-century tried to build an Ottoman nationalism, with limited democracy, against rising ethnic nationalism, and after their demise under Sultan Abdul Hamid II’s absolutist reign the Young Turks took up their legacy. Mustafa Kemal Atatürk spent his formative years in Hamidian Salonica and, in the army, joined the Committee of Union and Progress (CUP), which agitated for constitutional government; he abandoned Ottoman nationalism for Turkish nationalism and adopted a secular outlook.

Kept at arm’s length from power by rivals such as İsmail Enver and Ahmed Cemal, he could watch the CUP’s successes and failures. His defence of Gallipoli in World War I made his military career. After the Ottoman defeat he led the Turkish War of Independence against the Allies’ planned partition of Anatolia and Eastern Thrace, a war that was also a revolution: by 1923 his government in Ankara had abolished the Ottoman monarchy and proclaimed a Republic. Historian Şükrü Hanioğlu finds its roots in the Enlightenment ideas of the American and French revolutions, 19th-century positivism and republicanism. The politician Yakup Kadri Karaosmanoğlu used the word Kemalism on 28 June 1929 for “the basic principles and values of the Turkish path to modernity”.
sections.ideas:
Atatürk refused to be dogmatic and described his ideology as based on science and reason. Its six principles, symbolized by the Six Arrows, are republicanism, populism, nationalism, laicism, statism and reformism. Together they form a kind of Jacobinism, which Atatürk defined as using political despotism to break down the social despotism that, he believed, the bigotry of the ulema had fostered among the traditionally minded population. Republicanism replaced the Ottoman dynasty with popular sovereignty and elected government under the law: “Sovereignty belongs to the nation unrestrictedly and unconditionally.” Populism rejected class conflict in favour of class collaboration and national unity.

Laicism, close to French laïcité rather than the passive Anglo-American secularism, sought to banish religion from government and to bring the religious establishment under the state. Nationalism, drawing on Rousseau’s Social Contract, aimed to make a nation state from the remnants of the multi-ethnic Ottoman Empire, defining the Turkish nation as the people who established the Republic and promoting the motto “How happy is the one who says I am a Turk”; it renounced Pan-Turkism as an impossible goal. Statism had the state regulate the economy and invest where private enterprise would not, and reformism held the reforms irreversible, with no return to systems deemed backward.
sections.spread:
The Republican People’s Party (CHP), founded by Atatürk on 9 September 1923, ruled Turkey through a single-party period that lasted until 1950. The 1924 constitution called Turkey “republican, nationalist, attached to the people, interventionist, secular, and revolutionary”, and on 5 February 1937 the six principles were written into the constitution as state ideology. The CHP did not redefine its Kemalism between the 1940s and the 1960s; from the 1960s it moved toward the centre-left, and in the 1970s, amid a wider rejection of Kemalism in Turkish society, it adopted programmes labelled “democratic left”. The constitutions that followed the military coups of 1960 and 1980 kept its principles of secularism, nationalism and democracy.

Abroad, Turkey’s transformation was closely observed in Germany, France, Britain and the United States, and scholars have traced how Kemalism travelled as a practical model through interwar Bulgaria, Cyprus, Albania, Yugoslavia and Egypt, and on to Persia, Afghanistan, China and India. King Amanullah of Afghanistan, in 1928 the first head of state to visit the Republic officially, drew on it; Reza Shah of Iran accelerated his reforms after visiting Turkey in 1934, imposing Western dress for men and restricting the veil; and in Tunisia Habib Bourguiba’s Personal Status Code of 1956 closely mirrored Kemalist family law. The Bolsheviks saw the Kemalists as allies against Western imperialism.
sections.power:
In Atatürk’s fifteen years as president, sweeping reforms advanced a secular, republican and unitary state. The caliphate was abolished on 3 March 1924, and the office of Shaykh al-Islām gave way to a Presidency of Religious Affairs. In 1926 the mejelle and sharia codes were replaced by an adapted Swiss Civil Code and a penal code modelled on German and Italian law. Sufi orders and their lodges were dissolved, the titles of sheikh and dervish abolished, the fez penalized, all schools placed under one state curriculum, and the day of rest moved from Friday to Sunday. On 10 April 1928 the article naming Islam as the established religion was removed from the constitution. Turks had to adopt surnames and were not allowed to perform the hajj.

The regime promoted state support of the sciences and gender equality, purged Persian, Arabic and other loanwords from Turkish, and sponsored the Turkish History Thesis, with its ethno-racial ideas of Turkish origins in Central Asia; in 1931 it closed the Pan-Turkist Turkish Hearths. After the Great Depression an era of etatism built infrastructure, power stations and iron and steel industries, while the masses shouldered the burden of capital accumulation. Non-Muslims were often treated as second-class citizens, and the identity of the Kurds was denied for decades, with Kurds called “Mountain Turks”. In 1982, after the coup of 1980 by the Kemalist-leaning military, the constitution was amended to bar Islamic coverings from higher education.
sections.critiques:
Kemalism’s control of religion drew criticism from religious conservatives, who argued that a secular state could not control the activities of religious institutions; the policy was nonetheless adopted officially in the 1961 constitution. Its restrictions on personal choice reached religious duty and naming, and the ban on women’s Islamic coverings in higher education was publicly criticized by Joost Lagendijk, a member of the European Parliament who chaired its joint committee with Turkey, though the European Court of Human Rights has ruled in numerous cases that such restrictions do not violate human rights. In 2005 Article 301 of the penal code made it a crime to insult Turkishness; under pressure from the EU it was changed in 2008 to protect the “Turkish nation”.

Its nationalism has been criticized for its treatment of minorities. Kemalists saw non-Muslims as only nominal citizens, and in 1930 Atatürk called the names of citizens who thought of themselves as Kurds, Circassians, Laz or Bosnians “erroneous appellations”. Like the CUP, it can be said to have endorsed social Darwinism in some way, in wanting Turkish youth healthy and physically strong. Şükrü Hanioğlu calls it a “scientifically sanctioned version of Turkish nationalism” centred on Atatürk, who ruled as an enlightened autocrat bringing top-down change, and it rejected Western emancipatory ideologies such as liberalism and socialism. The Nazis viewed Kemalist Turkey as a “postgenocidal paradise” worthy of emulation, and Hitler called Mustafa Kemal the “star in the darkness”.
sections.legacy:
Kemalism remains the founding ideology of the Republic of Turkey. Its principles stand in the constitution, which since 1982 declares the Republic “loyal to the nationalism of Atatürk”, and its laicism holds that politicians may not claim to protect any religion or sect, a claim that is legal ground for the permanent banning of a party. Article 66 of the constitution carries the Kemalist notion of nationality: every citizen is recognized as a Turk, regardless of ethnicity, belief and gender. By the early 21st century most Kemalists, within the CHP or outside it, still believed in the original six principles, while others criticized its statist tendencies and sought to reduce them.

Scholarly interest in the transnational history of Kemalism has grown, from the interwar Balkans and Egypt to the Jewish community of British-ruled Palestine and the Muslim world further east, though most of that work, written in the countries concerned, views it positively and offers few critical insights. Scholars argue that Kemalism became a transnational political category through the circulations of the post-Ottoman space, carried not only by government but by material culture, ideas of gender and scientific debate. Those who view it positively link its secularism to the Enlightenment. It endures in the symbol of the Six Arrows and in the motto “How happy is the one who says I am a Turk”.

summary: Kemalism is the ideology of Mustafa Kemal Atatürk, founder of the Republic of Turkey in 1923, built on six principles: republicanism, populism, nationalism, laicism, statism and reformism. Its reforms abolished the caliphate and Islamic law and remade Turkish society on Western models, inspiring modernizers abroad, while its nationalism long denied Kurdish identity. It remains the Republic’s founding creed.
references: Toni Alaranta, Contemporary Kemalism: From Universal Secular-Humanism to Extreme Turkish Nationalism (Routledge, 2014)
Sinan Ciddi, Kemalism in Turkish Politics: The Republican People’s Party, Secularism and Nationalism (Routledge, 2009)
Doğan Gürpınar, “The Reinvention of Kemalism: Between Elitism, Anti-Elitism and Anti-Intellectualism”, Middle Eastern Studies 49 (2013)
Stefan Plaggenborg, Ordnung und Gewalt: Kemalismus – Faschismus – Sozialismus (Walter de Gruyter, 2012)
notes: Start 1923: the year of the Republic and of the CHP’s founding (9 September 1923); the word Kemalism is first dated to 28 June 1929 (Karaosmanoğlu), and the principles were “solidified” in 1937. 1929 would be the first-use alternative.
Region: given as Islamic Caliphates & Middle East; the article places it in Turkey (Anatolia).
The article gives Bozkurt only by surname; I did not add a first name.
Nutuk: the article names the speech but gives no year, so none is given.
The article mentions the Hat Law of 1925 only in passing (Reza Shah’s restrictions paralleled “Turkey’s 1925 Hat Law”); I wrote that the fez was penalized without a year.

Gender equality: the lede lists “gender equality” among the Atatürk-era policies, but the article gives no specific measure (no women’s suffrage, no dates), so I mentioned it only in general terms. The alphabet reform is not in the article (only the teaching of the Orkhon alphabet in Atatürk-era school books), so it is left out.
Single-party period “from 1923 to 1950” is from the Turkism section (“the single state period”).

The article has little sustained criticism; the critiques section gathers the points it does give (religious conservatives, Lagendijk, minorities, Hanioğlu, the Nazi admiration). The Nazi comparison is stated as the article states it, as their view.

Left out: the Hittites subsection (empty in the saved article), the full republican constitutional mechanics, the Turkish History Thesis’s school books, and the see-also variants (Left Kemalism, Liberal Kemalism, Post-Kemalism), which the article lists without text.
